evidence_contexts.source_text: ## Training Error and Generalization Error

Even with dropout and weight decay,
they remain so flexible that their ability to generalize to unseen data
cannot be explained via conventional learning-theoretic generalization guarantees.

However, the goal of deep learning (or more broadly, statistical inference) is to
reduce the generalization error.

The more formidable task is to find parameters
that will achieve low loss on data
that we have not seen before,
a challenge called *generalization*.

At the beginning of this chapter, we will describe
two methods that 
may improve model generalization, namely *image augmentation* and *fine-tuning*,
and apply them to image classification.

Thus we can decompose the task of fitting models into two key concerns:
(i) *optimization*: the process of fitting our models to observed data;
(ii) *generalization*: the mathematical principles and practitioners' wisdom
that guide as to how to produce models whose validity extends
beyond the exact set of data examples used to train them.
A hyperplane is a generalization to higher dimensions of a line or a plane.

effective_source_payload.proposed_definition_en: A model's ability to perform well on unseen data beyond the examples used for training.

evidence_contexts.source_text: ## The Matrix Factorization Model
Matrix Factorization :cite:`Koren.Bell.Volinsky.2009` is a well-established algorithm in the recommender systems literature.
Latent factor models such as matrix factorization are examples of model-based CF.
Although the final score was the result of an ensemble solution (i.e., a combination of many algorithms), the matrix factorization algorithm played a critical role in the final blend.

The first version of matrix factorization model is proposed by Simon Funk in a famous [blog
post](https://sifter.org/~simon/journal/20061211.html) in which he described the idea of factorizing the interaction matrix.
In this section, we will dive into the details of the matrix factorization model and its implementation.
This computation is important in an area called matrix factorization.
# Matrix Factorization
Synthetic: In this chapter, matrix factorization predicts user–item preferences by learning latent factors from an interaction matrix.

Thus, we need to compute the expected risk that we incur as the loss function,
i.e., we need to multiply the probability of the outcome
with the benefit (or harm) associated with it.
When we train high-capacity models we run the risk of overfitting.

In other words, the effect of the uncertain risk
outweighs the benefit by far.
We risk losing information in the cropped out portions.

As described
in :numref:`subsec_empirical-risk-and-risk`,
the empirical risk
is an average loss
on the training dataset
while the risk is the expected loss 
on the entire population of data.

For example, if we were training a model to predict
the risk that a loan defaults,
we might associate each applicant with a vector
whose components correspond to their income,
length of employment, number of previous defaults, and other factors.
The second one has a much larger degree of fluctuation, and thus represents a much larger risk.

In sensitive applications of machine learning,
like predictive policing, resume screening, and risk models used for lending,
we must be especially alert to the consequences of garbage data.
